prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, which opened the way to timekeeping at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Having read the opening ballots, I move my preferred configuration from B044 (my own first place) to B007. Seven of eight members ranked optical lattice clocks, six of them in the top three and three of them first, and the scientific case holds up on my own reading. The magic-wavelength idea (Katori) removes the light shift that would otherwise forbid trapping the atoms, and the Katori and Ye programmes took neutral-atom clocks to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. Several independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST) reproduce and intercompare these clocks. The platform is already used for tests of fundamental constants, searches for new physics, relativistic geodesy and the roadmap to a redefined second. The two-name attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist, with a concept and first demonstration on one side and the record-accuracy and many-body programme on the other. As a theorist I also judge it a discovery of real physics, since a clock this good turns gravitational redshift over millimetres into a laboratory observable. I still think circuit QED is a foundational achievement. But I accept that the committee is better served by the candidate with broad support that is also mature and cleanly attributable.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that optical clocks sit close to the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems, which included Wineland's ion clocks. A committee could read the lattice clock as an incremental refinement of recognised metrology and not a new discovery. Katori's and Ye's contributions also rest on a wider base of work (Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, the Lemonde and PTB groups), and the ion-clock lineage is outside this candidate's credited names. The citation therefore has to be worded so that the lattice concept, and not clock accuracy in general, is what is rewarded. Recognition is also arguably premature while the redefinition of the second is still pending, although I do not think the physics depends on it.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B007 first as precision measurement at its most fundamental, and he notes that the ion-clock work honoured in 2012 and the 2005 comb prize could be argued to overlap.
responses.response: I agree on merit and have moved toward your ranking. On overlap I would go further than you do. The 2012 prize recognised the control and measurement of individual quantum systems, with the ion clocks as an application, and the 2005 prize recognised the comb as the tool for counting optical frequencies. Neither introduced a scheme for interrogating many neutral atoms in a lattice with the trap perturbation cancelled by design. That is the invention the citation should name. I am less sure than you that Katori's proposal and the first experimental clock can be cleanly separated. Katori did both, so I do not see a case for crediting the theoretical proposal separately.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene (B005) first, as a conceptually clean prediction followed by a discovery, and puts B007 second on importance and clarity.
responses.response: I agree that B005 is a strong candidate and I keep it as my first alternative. Where I differ is on maturity. You call the flat-band and correlated-insulator phenomenology well established, and I accept that. But a prize citation would also have to say something about the superconductivity, and its pairing mechanism is not agreed. The attribution is also less settled than for B007: Cao and other experimental groups, and earlier twisted-bilayer theory, are not covered by the three credited names. If the committee wants a condensed-matter prize this year I would not object to B005. I just think the clock prize carries less interpretive and attribution risk.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B007 first and puts circuit QED (B044) only seventh, partly because of the 2025 prize and the unresolved Blais/Girvin allocation.
responses.response: This is the argument that moved me most. I had judged B044 distinct from the 2025 award, since the 2025 prize was about macroscopic quantum tunnelling and energy quantisation in a circuit, and cQED is about coupling an artificial atom to a resonator for readout and gates. I still believe that. But two prizes on superconducting circuits in two consecutive years would be hard to defend, and you are right that the four-name cut to three is a real injustice whichever name is dropped. I do not agree that B044 is only a seventh-place candidate. It is the architecture behind almost every present quantum processor, and the committee should come back to it later. I no longer think it is the right choice for this year.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks anyonic statistics (B001) first as a conceptually deep prediction that experiments around 2020 realised, while noting that the experimental credit is unresolved.
responses.response: I share your admiration for the Leinaas-Myrheim idea, and I put B001 eighth for two reasons, not because of a doubt about its importance. First, the 2020 interferometer and collider experiments are recent and their interpretation is still being scrutinised. Second, six credited names do not fit within three places, and you yourself say the experimental leg is not cleanly resolved. Wilczek and Halperin are also absent from the credited names, which weakens a theory-credit configuration. Heiblum, Fève and Manfra each have a serious claim, and a prize that must choose among them now would look arbitrary. I would be more comfortable with B001 if non-Abelian statistics were established, but that has not happened.

responses.point: Pearce ranks B007 first as a genuine instrument breakthrough with a repeatedly demonstrated payoff, and places circuit QED fifth, mainly because of the proximity to the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I agree with your instrument-breakthrough framing and with your reading that the multi-laboratory reproduction of lattice clocks is decisive for maturity. I would add that the same criteria favour B044 on reproducibility, so what separates the two this year is timing and balance across fields, not merit. I note that you list Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf where I list Schoelkopf, Wallraff and Girvin. That difference shows the attribution problem in B044 and is another reason I do not press it now.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads lattice clocks as a new invention or as a refinement of metrology already honoured in 2005 and 2012.
Whether a third name from the lattice-clock community should be considered, which the supplied credit does not cover.
Whether a circuit-QED prize in a later year is still appropriate, and which of Blais and Girvin should hold the theory place among four credited names.
I rely on recalled priority history and have not verified exact dates or significance levels.
statement.conflict_note: I direct WACQT and work at Chalmers, where Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson are colleagues and Anton Frisk Kockum is a frequent co-author. Chalmers also hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize. My own work on superconducting circuits, circuit and waveguide QED and quantum-computing theory is close to B044, and to a lesser extent B031, so I should recuse myself from, or at least discount my own view on, those candidates. I have no connection to Katori or Ye, to the B007 community, or to the other shortlisted candidates in the supplied profile.
